nameStory: The 'green poinsettia' name comes from its resemblance to the familiar holiday plant, especially when its upper leaves turn pale green or yellowish around the tiny flowers. Unlike the bright red Christmas poinsettia, this wild cousin keeps things more subtle with its greenish display. The scientific name 'dentata' means 'toothed,' referring to the jagged edges of its leaves.
description: Green poinsettia is a hairy annual wildflower that grows 8-20 inches tall with an upright or slightly leaning stem. Its pointed, lance-shaped leaves have distinctly toothed edges and feel fuzzy to the touch from all the fine hairs covering the plant. The tiny cream or yellowish flowers cluster at the branch tips, surrounded by pale green bracts that give this spurge its poinsettia-like appearance. It produces small, three-lobed seed capsules about the size of a pea.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves with distinctly toothed edges, covered in soft hairs that make them feel fuzzy when touched. They're arranged alternately along the stem and are typically 1-3 inches long.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny cream or pale yellow flowers just a few millimeters wide, clustered at branch tips and surrounded by pale greenish bracts that create a poinsettia-like effect.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright or slightly leaning annual herb with noticeably hairy stems and leaves, giving the entire plant a soft, fuzzy texture.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Three-lobed capsules about half an inch wide that split open to reveal three bumpy, rounded seeds. The capsules may be somewhat heart-shaped.

habitat: Green poinsettia is quite rare in New England, with only a few documented sightings. When found, it typically grows in disturbed soils, waste areas, and along roadsides where other weedy plants thrive. It prefers sunny, open locations with well-drained soil.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as weather warms, producing the first fuzzy leaves. Young plants are small and may be easily overlooked among other emerging weeds.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and begin flowering, with the characteristic pale green bracts becoming most noticeable. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing seeds. Plants begin to decline as cooler weather arrives, eventually dying with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, green poinsettia dies completely in winter, surviving only as seeds in the soil waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: Like all spurges, green poinsettia produces a milky white sap when broken that can cause skin irritation and was once used to remove warts - but don't try this at home, as the sap can also cause painful blisters!
confusionNotes: The fuzzy, toothed leaves help distinguish green poinsettia from other spurges, which typically have smoother leaves. The hairy texture is usually noticeable even from a distance, making the plant look softer and more gray-green than most of its spurge relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, green poinsettia is only distantly related to the familiar Christmas poinsettia houseplant, though both belong to the large spurge family. Its native range is uncertain, and it's considered a noxious weed in some areas due to its ability to spread and potentially harm livestock.
compareHints: Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves. The fuzzy texture and jagged leaf edges make it quite different from common relatives like spotted spurge or cypress spurge. The pale green bracts around its flowers are also more prominent than in most other spurge species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
